items.title: 68002_Benny Waters oral history interview
items.q: my inspiration was Coleman Hawkins, it was that slap tongue.

ctx.x: I mean, those are '27, we're talking about 1918. So I'm trying to get a parallel line of thinking. Now I understand that you're saying it's the same thing in that there's a principle involved of using the chords. And you're using it for solos in 1918, you're using it for solos in 1982. But something's gotta be different, I mean because you probably weren't up to your 1927 level in 1918 and you're saying here in '82 that '27 is way behind. So I mean, how good were you playing, what -

Well, I could, I could have been playin' better first thing if I was playin' alto, that's the first thing. And that was my first instrument, and I was better on alto than I was on tenor. That's the first thing. And I could have been playing better construction of harmonies and things on the alto at that period. Then in the meantime, when I made those records with Charlie Johnson at that, at down in Camden at Victor, my inspiration was Coleman Hawkins, it was that slap tongue. You can even hear it on the record, I…

better because I was changed to a horn that I wasn't even familiar with, see what I mean? Very well, very easily be playing more. I don't know, people have all kinds of things 'cause I've advanced a lot by listening. But I still think I play alto better. I think I'm more handy with the alto, I still think so. Well, that's proof that I know what I'm talking from beginning back there, I'm now, today - I think I'm more handy with the alto. I do more tricks, I can get over the horn, I can even play more modern, if…

items.title: Benny Waters interviewed by Michael Woods, Los Angeles, California, September 1, 1995
items.q: And on tenor, there was no one in that period but Coleman Hawkins. Because he was the greatest of all at that period, see?

ctx.x: Well this can be explained, I’ll tell you why, because I don’t never get tired of listening, you know? And I listen to everybody, everything. I listen to free jazz. I listen to bebop. I listen to fusion. And I find I get something from everything. Dixieland. I worked in a Dixieland band three years at Jimmy Ryan’s. So, I worked in a blues band, see for a year and a half. So I didn’t like the band so well, see but the guy liked me so I stayed there see until I got tired and I left. But if it seems that I play…

Not exclusive, but I made several arrangements for him, see? And then the next was Benny Carter, the young Benny Carter. That’s on alto. And on tenor, there was no one in that period but Coleman Hawkins. Because he was the greatest of all at that period, see? Then you listen to everybody else, see, so you can get something from everybody.
